The best wireless earbuds weve ever tested (and continue to love)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're looking for a new pair of earbuds, we have good news: You have a lot of options.
  • In a recent development, while you can still find wired earbuds that plug in and go, the market is flooded with high-quality wireless options.
  • These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're looking for a new pair of earbuds, we have good news: You have a lot of options. The bad news? You have a lot of options, and your decision can get overwhelming, fast. Wasn't life easier when iPhones came with a free pair of earbuds?

In a recent development, while you can still find wired earbuds that plug in and go, the market is flooded with high-quality wireless options. Now, you'll find models with advanced active noise cancellation, multi-point pairing, high-resolution audio support, and extra-long battery life. To help you choose, Mashable's audio experts put the best wireless earbuds from Apple, Bose, Sony, and other top brands to the test.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Industry observers note that the best wireless earbuds range anywhere from $10 to $1,000, especially if you're going for professional-grade studio earphones. And if you care about active noise cancellation, you can easily spend $300 — that's the price of peace and quiet. You can also get hyperspecialized models like sleep earbuds, bone-conduction earbuds for working out, and open earbuds for transparency. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

In 2026, our top picks for earbuds are the Sony WF-1000XM6, Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd gen), and Panasonic Technics AZ100s, which provide outstanding sound quality and ANC. But keep in mind that these models will run you $299 to $329. While we stand by the value of everything on this list, we know that spending over $300 on a pair of earbuds is a lot to stomach. That's why we've also included more budget-friendly wireless earbuds under $100 that still deliver excellent performance.

It has been revealed that ready to start shopping now? Here are our favorite wireless and noise-cancelling earbuds as of November 2026.

Read our full review of the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds.

It has been revealed that anyone looking for the all-around best experience: Sony's new XM6 earbuds are the follow-up we've been waiting for from the brand. Though they cost a lot, they justify their price point in an excellent performance on all fronts, which brings some of the best ANC, sound quality, design, and ease of use to one elegant package.

Sony built a reputation for providing some of the best sound quality available in the game, and while we still think the Technics on this list eke out a better performance, Sony's overall package is unrivaled.

Sources indicate that the earbuds sound great out of the box, but the 10-band equalizer gives the user plenty of options for customization. Whether we listened to classic rock or straight-up classical concertos, these earbuds made music sound immersive, rich, and clear. To supplement the great sound quality, Sony also stepped up its ANC game from the previous gen, resulting in the best ANC we've ever encountered on a pair of earbuds. Though we wish it were adjustable (especially at this price point), if you're looking to block out the world around you as much as possible, we think these perform even better than our former favorites, the Bose QC Ultra 2 buds.

In a recent development, where Bose has Sony beat is in comfort. Sony did redesign the shape of its earbuds from the previous gen, helping provide an even more comfortable and flush fit. Still, Bose's stability band still takes the cake for the best fit we've ever experienced — but Sony is closing that comfort gap.

Read our full review of the Panasonic Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds.

Industry observers note that audiophiles first and foremost: If you want to hear every note in perfect crisp detailed sound, the Panasonic's Technics EAH-AZ100 make music better thanks to their magnetic fluid drivers. Whether you want a fully customizable experience by adjusting your bass and treble, or you just want to pop in your buds and experience delicious spatial audio without the fuss, the Technics offer customers both.

Sources indicate that panasonic blew us away with its Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds. If you've ever thought that earbuds can't deliver the same potent sound quality as over-ear headphones, then let the AZ100s prove you wrong. The buds come with four different ear tips that range from extra small to large, delivering a snug and secure fit suitable for even those with small or narrow ears who struggle to find earbuds that fit. That being mentioned, they aren't the most comfortable headphones we've ever tested (nothing beats the Bose QuietComfort Ultras), as they get uncomfortable after a couple of hours of wear.

Sources indicate that however, what you're really after here is the incredible sound quality of the Technics. Music just sounds better on the AZ100 earbuds. The earbuds deliver music as close to the source as possible. While listening to James Brown's "The Boss," the song sounded rich and textured, with layers of horn and deep bass bursting through. Plus, it picks up on the most subtle details, like in "Angel Of My Dreams" by Jade, the soft shuttering of cameras flashing on the backing track rang through in crisp detail.

Plus, these headphones have impressive active noise cancellation. While testing them on a trip to Upcoming York, they blocked out the clatter of the subway and ruckus of noisy streets. With such excellent ANC, nothing distracts from the superior audio quality. The three-way multipoint connection is another huge advantage of these headphones. I could seamlessly switch between my iPhone, iPad, and MacBook Pro without having to open the app.

According to recent reports, not to mention, these earbuds have killer battery life. They last for 10 hours with an additional 28 hours available with the charging case.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds (2nd gen).

Long-haul travelers, students, or anyone who can't get earbuds to fit quite right: For those who value noise cancellation and all-day wear above all else, the $299 Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds (2nd gen) are worth the investment. With spatial audio and some of the best ANC we've encountered, these earbuds deliver immersive sound that envelopes you in your music.

Over-ear headphones are the typical pick for those who want the best noise cancellation, but these days, you're no longer limited if you prefer earbuds but still want top-tier ANC.

Bose's second iteration of its QuietComfort Ultra earbuds doesn't change too much from the original, with the main improvements coming in the form of wireless charging, improved speech clarity on calls, and better adaptive ANC, but we also noticed some minor improvements to the sound profile, which also did a great job of sounding full and resonant right out of the box.

Sources indicate that where these earbuds really shine, however, is in their name: it's their fit and noise cancellation. Though they only have three sizes of ear tips and stability bands, the design of these earbuds allows for a fit that's both secure and comfortable enough to wear for hours on end, which isn't a given with earbuds. The noise cancellation impresses, too, even without any music playing, thanks to the eight microphones packed into these buds. Common household sounds like air conditioning, neighbors, and other people existing in your space all but disappear with the ANC bumped all the way up. If you don't like that much blockage, you can turn on transparency mode or manually adjust the level of ANC.

Recent findings suggest that so what are the downsides? Besides being priced like a premium pair of earbuds (which, to be fair, they are in their performance), the six-hour battery life is starting to lag behind competitors. Plus, the equalizer is less sophisticated than what you'll find on other earbuds, and the touch controls weren't quite as seamless as we want on $300 earbuds. Still, for the combo of noise-cancelling and comfort, we can't choose a better pair of earbuds.

Read our full review of the Apple AirPods Pro 3.

Apple fans: Apple device owners will appreciate how easily these earbuds pair with multiple devices, as well as their impressive active noise cancellation and the many ways they can be used.

The AirPods Pro pop up on most best of lists, and though we've always been fans, the third generation takes these earbuds to a latest level.

At the most basic level, these earbuds perform well in all the ways you'd want them to: the sound profile is robust and clear, the noise cancellation truly silences the world around you, and they pair easily to Apple devices. With this generation, Apple bumped up these buds' battery life to eight hours per charge, putting them firmly on the higher end of what's available on the market.

It has been revealed that then, there are the extra features. Apple included a built-in heart rate monitor, which can be used when you track your workouts with the Fitness app. How did it perform? "Perfectly," according to Mashable contributor Adam Doud's review. "I checked the heart rate against another device...and in every instance, the heart rate from the AirPods Pro 3 was within a beat or two per minute of the other device, so that speaks very well for its accuracy." Along with the IP57 water- and sweat-resistance and five sizes of ear tips for finding just the right fit, the AirPods Pro have become a much better pair of earbuds for working out this generation.

Finally, the live translation. At the time of writing, it's available in English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and English from the UK. Doud wrote that it worked fairly accurately (as compared to movie subtitles) with a one to two second delay, making the feature viable for real-time use.

Sources indicate that at $249, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are on par (and even cheaper) than other premium competitors. So what's the catch? Well, for anyone looking to fine-tune their own audio experience, there's no companion app or custom equalizer, but for everything else you get, the trade-off may well be worth it.

Read our full review of the AirPods 5 with wireless charging case.

Apple fans on a budget: The AirPods Pro 3 are great, but with the addition of better noise cancellation, a wireless charging case, volume controls on the stem, and live translation to the AirPods 5 model, you can get a very similar experience for $100 cheaper, making this the best value option for Apple-centric users.

These are also a great pick for anyone who wants earbuds that sit in between an in-ear and open earbud, as they don't have an ear tip that's situated in the ear canal, but rather rest near it as a traditional earbud would.

Apple pulled a rare move by lowering the prices on the AirPods 5 while adding more features, which made our job pretty easy in recommending them. They come with 50 percent better ANC than the AirPods 4, while being $149 compared to the 4's $179. Despite being a semi-in-ear model, they provide a surprising amount of sound control. Mashable Senior Editor Stan Schroeder wrote in his review that though they struggled on higher-pitched sounds, "on an actual plane, I realized they did a pretty good job of reducing both the engines' drone and the passengers' chatter.".

He was also particularly impressed by how they sounded for live performances, as open earbuds tend to let the wider soundstage shine more than traditional in-ear buds, which might emphasize clarity and bass — he appreciated the width of the sound. These earbuds also come with the Live Translation feature found on the AirPods Pro 3, which allows for language translation in real time, as well as a volume sliding control on the stem. You'll miss out on the more expensive earbuds' built-in heart rate monitor and Hearing Protection feature, but if neither is too important to you, you'd likely be better off saving the cash. The biggest difference besides the wear is perhaps the battery life: where the AirPods Pro 3 get eight hours per charge, you'll have to settle for five hours per charge with the AirPods 5, but you will have a smaller carrying case than the Pros.

Sources indicate that bargain hunters: Finding a solid pair of budget earbuds is all about balance, and the EarFun Air Pro 4 exemplify that perfectly. While not the absolute cheapest pair of earbuds you could buy, they're still less than $100 and perform at the level of earbuds double their price. For anyone looking for the best value noise-cancelling earbuds, these are our top pick.

The EarFun earbuds don't fall into the pitfalls of other budget buds on the market. Yeah, you'll pay more than $50 pair (but only slightly if you grab them during one of their frequent sales). What you'll get in return is affordable earbuds that can adeptly handle a multipoint connection, feature a well-rounded sound profile with variation thanks to the in-app equalizer, and a battery life that can likely power you through most, if not all, of your workday.

The efficacy of the active noise cancellation is an especially standout feature of these earbuds, thanks to the absence noise breakthrough or strong hissing to supplement the power of the ANC. (Usually, one or both can be found on cheaper earbuds.) EarFun could've stopped there, but these earbuds also offer manually adjustable ANC, which isn't even a given on premium noise-cancelling earbuds. While not every level of adjustment is worth writing home about, it's still a nice addition.

It has been revealed that five sizes of ear tips ranging from XS to XL help with a comfortable fit and providing the best passive noise cancellation possible. Overall, these earbuds start to verge on too good to be true for their price point. The one major flaw we could find is that their on-ear touch controls verged on being both under-and overly sensitive, causing our tester to prefer toggling them off entirely in the companion app. Still, if there was one feature EarFun was going to flop on, this is maybe the least annoying of the bunch.

Read our full review of the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special earbuds.

Sources indicate that restless sleepers in noisy nighttime environments: Within a few months, Soundcore turned around and upgraded its already excellent Sleep A30 earbuds, bringing the Sleep A30 Special earbuds to the scene. For anyone who needs noise cancellation to help them get to sleep, the Sleep A30 Specials are basically your only option — thankfully, they're also one of the best valued options.

The major names in the sleep earbuds space are Ozlo and Soundcore. While Ozlo is known for being made by former Bose engineers, the $349 earbuds come at a huge price point — especially considering their lack of features in comparison to Soundcore's offerings.

In a recent development, most notably, the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special earbuds offer active noise cancellation, the only sleep earbuds to do that other than their predecessor, the Sleep A30 earbuds. Even better, they do it at a significantly lower price point than the Ozlo buds at $229.99. While it's still a decent price to pay for earbuds solely designed for sleep, relatively speaking, A30 Specials offer some of the best value by far due to the feature set.

In a recent development, in addition to the ANC, the companion app offers several white noise options, including customizable soundscapes and Calm app meditations. If you prefer to stream your own audio, Soundcore's Bluetooth streaming with ANC on can last through an entire night of sleep (an upgrade from the regular A30 earbuds). The brand also recently added an revision to the app that allows customers to toggle on a timed turn-off for their audio, instead of the sleep detection option that existed at the earbuds' release.

These earbuds' case also monitors the environment in real time to provide adaptive snore masking, should the user toggle that option on. Standard features that exist on other earbuds will also be found on these buds, including a built-in alarm, sleep tracking data, and touch controls.

Read our full review of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds.

It has been revealed that runners, gym rats, and fitness fans: If you don't want to be bothered by loose or ill-fitting headphones while lifting or on a run, go for a pair that won't budge. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 fit snuggly within the ear, but the extra ear hook adds an extra level of security. For iOS people, these connect instantly, but even Android users can benefit from a quick Bluetooth connection, too.

When you're on the go and want to stay hands-free, the Powerbeats Pro 2 have external controls for answering calls or playing music. Plus, the Powerbeats bring crisp sound that helps you block out sound when you'd rather focus on your workout and not the gym crowd around you. Not to mention, the Powerbeats also include a heart rate monitor for real-time readings.

The Powerbeats Pro have earned a permanent spot in my gym bag. They fit snuggly within the ear and with the ear hooks don't budge, no matter how sweaty I get or how I move through my workouts. As an iPhone user, they're a dream to connect, automatically doing so whenever I take them out of the case.

With their noise-cancelling capabilities, they're able to block out the noise of the gym or the outdoors. But if you want to be able to hear the world around you for safety, you can swap into Transparency Mode. The sound is clear and consistent. Is it the best sound quality I've tested? No, but it's still pretty great.

Recent findings suggest that the on-ear earbud controls are great. The Beats Fit Pro suffered from overly sensitive controls, causing me to accidentally end a call or two. But the controls on the Powerbeats Pro 2 don't get set off by accidentally brushing them. The battery life on the Powerbeats Pro 2 is incredible, up to 45 hours with the case. I think I went a full month without charging them — even with daily use.

It actually wasn't love at first wear with the Powerbeats. At first, they're pretty awkward figuring out how to fit the bud in your ear and then hooking them around. Both my colleague, Bethany Allard, and I tested the Powerbeats and struggled with the learning curve of getting them to fit, and it was a bad first impression of the Beats. While I do like how customizable they are with five different ear tips, navigating their fit is difficult at first.

However, after a few months of use, I realized the Powerbeats Pro 2 became my go-to gym earbud. While other earbuds didn't sound as good, started to slip out when things got sweaty, or required frequent charging, I always returned to the Powerbeats Pro 2.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort earbuds.

Anyone who wants budget-friendly from a premium brand: If you want good-quality sound but don’t want to spend over $200, the Bose QuietComfort is an affordable answer to the brand’s lineup. They’re focused on a great fit, as they not only come with multiple ear tips but multiple bands that can be changed out on the earbuds for a better fit on the crest of your ear.

Sources indicate that the accompanying app lets you adjust audio levels, but you won’t need to, as these earbuds make all your music sound better. They’re reliable, have a long battery life, and are sure to please the pickiest of audiophiles.

It has been revealed that I’ve sung the praises of the QuietComfort Ultra, but Bose’s latest earbuds, the entry-level QuietComfort, are also fantastic, especially with their under-$200 price tag. Even after adjusting the ear tips and bands, I didn’t find the fit on these quite as secure as the Ultras. However, my colleague Bethany Allard, who also tested the QuietComfort earbuds, said they were the best earbuds that have ever fit her.

The QuietComfort’s sound quality is just phenomenal. With these earbuds, listening to Ethel Cain’s A House in Nebraska immersed me in the orchestrations. When Brick House by The Commodores came on, the earbuds elevated the snappy drum beats so that I may have been listening live.

The noise cancellation on the QuietComfort earbuds isn’t as sophisticated as the Ultras; I found they had more sound leakage and that classic ANC buzz when I was in noisy environments. However, the ANC on these is still great, especially in quiet spaces.

It has been revealed that one tiny beef I have with the Bose QuietComfort earbuds is that they require a different app than the standard Bose one. This is annoying if you’re an existing Bose user and need to download another app; plus, this earbud app just isn’t as good as Bose’s flagship app.

All in all, these are a solid pair of headphones that, for $179, are an unbeatable value.

Read our full review of the Bose Ultra Open (2nd gen).

Sources indicate that anyone who finds earbuds too uncomfortable: If you want a pair of everyday earbuds with an open design, the latest Bose Ultra Open earbuds will be your best bet. Yes, $300 is a hefty investment, but they have the best sound quality of any open earbuds we've tried. Plus, Bose's clip-on design can't be beat, from the comfort to the colorways.

The open earbuds trend has taken off in the past few years for anyone who craves some more awareness when listening to their audio. Maybe it's because you don't want to totally feel siloed in your own world; maybe it's convenient for exercise, more comfortable, or simply safer with their heightened awareness. Whatever your reason for wearing them, in our testing, we found the second-generation Bose Ultra Open earbuds are the best choice for most folks.

Recent findings suggest that we were already fans of the sound quality of the first-generation Bose open buds, but the second generation adds more bass and depth, making it the superior open earbud listening experience. Bose also nails the design. The clip is secure, easy to adjust, and comfortable enough to wear for hours. You'd think at least one of those areas would suffer, but Bose strikes the balance. Rounding out the top-tier design are the excellent color selection (black, white smoke, limited-edition cherry chocolate, olive green, and sky pink) and the best tactile controls you'll find on any pair of earbuds, thanks to the button on the top of the clip mechanism's back side. These buds also come with an IPX4 water and sweat resistance rating, so you're cleared for workouts.

So what's the catch? Well, they're expensive as hell, even for regular noise-cancelling earbuds. If these lean too pricey, our former top pick, the Shokz OpenDots One, is still a worthwhile (and more affordable) choice for clip-on earbuds.

Read our full review of the Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro.

It has been revealed that versatility is key: The Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro are the jack of all (earbud) trades, master of none. They're the only real option if you want to keep open and noise cancelling earbuds with you on the go without carrying around, or paying or, two completely separate pairs of earbuds. They're not the best in either department, but they're pretty solid in both, making them an excellent option for those who value convenience above all else.

Admittedly, the pool of options is pretty much limited to the AeroFit 2 Pro when considering dual-form earbuds — unless you count the noise-reduction features on Shokz OpenFit Pro. For true noise cancellation and open form wear however, you'll have to look to the Soundcore buds.

It has been revealed that that criteria on its own doesn't earn these earbuds a spot on our list, though. Soundcore followed through on their innovative design by producing earbuds that actually perform well, too, even with their flaws. Let's start with the weakest point: these earbuds don't come with interchangeable ear tips (á la the AirPods 4), instead staying in place with an adjustable ear hook that looks them into the noise cancelling or open mode. While still relatively comfortable, it does mean that they suffer somewhat on the passive noise cancellation front. Paired with just-okay ANC, you won't be getting the best noise blocking out there — expect to be able to somewhat make out conversations of coworkers or fellow cafe-goers, though both will be dampened.

Industry observers note that still, if the best ANC isn't a top priority, this a fairly easy feature to overlook. Especially when a quick adjustment of the ear hook, you suddenly have the best transparency mode possible — an open-ear design. Soundcore has plenty of experience making solid open earbuds, so it came as no surprise that the sound on these was clear, relatively robust, and noticeably varied, especially with equalizer adjustments. The ear hook kept them sturdy and in place, making these IP55 dust and water-resistance rated buds an excellent option for wear while working out or simply staying aware while out and about.

In a recent development, there are two overarching types of earbuds: wireless and wired. While those descriptors are self-explanatory, let's get into the specifics of both.

Wireless earbuds connect to devices via Bluetooth for cordless usage. These earbuds range from $20 budget models to high-end models with active noise cancellation. While they don't require a wire to connect to a device, some wireless earbuds still have a wire that might go around the back of the neck to connect the buds.

While earbuds traditionally don't provide the passive noise cancellation of over-the-ear headphones, wireless models often feature ANC, which electronically blocks out background noise. With wireless headphones, you need to consider the battery life. Most models should have an eight-hour or more battery life before they need to be recharged.

Wired earbuds are the original model: two buds connected by a wire to your audio source. While they once felt high-tech, they're pretty basic now. Wired earbuds with active noise cancellation are basically non-existent, other than Bose's newest release.

The biggest positive of wired headphones is that they don't need to be charged. They're a great backup option to keep in your bag in case your usual wireless headphones or earbuds run out of charge.

We added the new Apple AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case to this guide in October following their September 2026 release as a cheaper alternative for Apple users, or for folks who don't prefer the ear tip fit of the AirPods Pro 3.

It has been revealed that after extensive testing, Mashable Lead Shopping Reporter Bethany Allard rounded up the best sleep earbuds. You can read her full guide, but as of February 2026, we've added the Anker Soundcore Sleep A30 Special to this guide, which Allard says are the best sleep earbuds for most people. Also in February 2026, we added the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds as our top pick for the best overall earbud, and removed the previous generation, the WF-1000XM5, as the best Sony earbud.

Bose recently revealed two latest open earbuds: the Ultra Open (2nd gen) and Sport Open. We'll be testing them out to see how they compare to the Shokz earbuds in this guide. Bose also released a new pair of wired noise-cancelling earbuds, which are a breakthrough in the wired earbuds market.

With the announcement that Bose is acquiring Skullcandy and the release of the Noise Master Buds Open earbuds with Sound by Bose, we'll be testing more Bose-powered audio products not directly from the brand.

If you're just looking for a pair of everyday wireless earbuds, all but one of the models in this guide will check that box. (We formerly included the Marshall Mode earbuds for folks who preferred a wired option, but have since removed them from our guide as the version we tested is difficult to find in stock these days.).

Industry observers note that if you're looking for the highest quality wireless earbuds, you can't go wrong with the Sony WF-1000XM6, Bose QuietComfort Ultra, Apple AirPods Pro 3, and Panasonic Technics EAH-AZ100 earbuds, our most recent recommendations in 2026. All of these wireless earbuds feature elite noise cancellation, stellar sound, long battery life, and a comfortable fit for extended wear.

Though most earbuds are now wireless, this ultimately comes down to preference. If you have a tighter budget or don't want to worry about the battery running low all the time, wired earbuds are a great option. With that mentioned, it is significantly harder to find wired earbuds with active noise cancellation. At the time of writing, the only pair with both wired connectivity and ANC both is from Bose — we're still in the process of testing them out.

Recent findings suggest that to help you decide, we put a range of wireless earbuds to the test to determine which are worth your money. Whether you're simply looking for earbuds to get you through the work day, a pair to take with you on a flight, or a pair that you can live in 24/7, we have a set of buds for you. And if nothing on this list stands out to you, you can always expand your search to headphones as well.

Recent findings suggest that as long as they're Bluetooth-compatible, these earbuds should connect to any smartphone, tablet, or laptop regardless of operating system. All of the earbuds on this list work equally well across iOS and Android systems with one exception — Apple AirPods.

Our favorite AirPods, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are great and will connect to an Android device, but you won't get the same ease of connectivity or full array of features. However, other earbuds like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra earbuds and the Panasonic Technics AZ100 feature Android apps so you can experience their full range of features on an Android device.

According to recent reports, each pair of earbuds selected for this guide was hands-on tested by a Mashable reporter, editor, or contributor. Along with wireless earbuds tested specifically for this article, we also combed through our existing reviews to pick the best of the best earbuds for 2026. In addition to the bang for your buck, when testing earbuds, we consider criteria such as:.

For each of our earbuds, we do our best to run their battery life out and test it against the stated battery life. All ANC earbuds are used with ANC, and while each tester defers to their preferred volume, we do try to average around the 50% mark when in use.

We tested out these earbuds with a variety of songs, from live performances to bass-heavy electronic music, R&B, rock, and folksy guitar songs. We evaluated how they sounded out of the box, along with any EQ presets or custom controls. Realistically, you'll make calls when using your earbuds, which is why we put each of these earbuds through a call test, making sure the person on the other end of the phone could hear us clearly and consistently.

Sources indicate that though this category can be subjective, we made sure each of our selections at least had several different ear tip sizes and were comfortable to wear for stretches of three hours or more. We also evaluate features like cleverly placed touch controls and stabilizers for keeping earbuds in place, both during casual use and exercise.

Any feature that made the earbuds stand out and also performed consistently well earned points in this category. For example, in addition to a rich out-of-the box sound profile, the Sony earbuds had an incredibly customizable and user-friendly experience with the in-app equalizer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Full Moon is here, and this one's a Supermoon. That means the Moon is closer to Earth than usual, making it appear slightly bigger and brighter in the night sky.

According to recent reports, as of Tuesday, Nov. 24, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Full Moon phase, with 100% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Imbrium and Crisium, as well as the Copernicus Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Archimedes Crater, the Endymion Crater, and the Alphonsus Crater. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 15 landing spot, the Schiller Crater, and the Rima Hyginus.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

In a recent development, it takes around 29.5 days for the Moon to move through all its phases, according to NASA. Throughout this period, the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun determines how much of its illuminated surface we can see. Starting with a New Moon, the visible portion gradually increases until it reaches a Full Moon, before shrinking again as the cycle comes back around.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

It has been revealed that first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Recent findings suggest that waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Sources indicate that so, when can you see November's Full Moon? Here's when it will reach peak illumination and why it's called the Beaver Moon.

The Full Moon will peak at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, Nov. 24, according to Time and Date.

In a recent development, according to Royal Museums Greenwich, there is some debate over the source of November's Full Moon name. Some theories suggests it dates back to a time when Native American communities would set traps for beavers in November. However, others link it to more generally to the animals' preparations for winter around this time.

Sources indicate that in North America, the next Full Moon will take place on December 23. However, due to time zone differences, in other parts of the world it will will fall on December 24.

In a recent development, the Moon's appearance changes throughout its orbit around Earth as different amounts of its sunlit side become visible to us. This repeating cycle takes about 29.5 days and is divided into eight distinct phases. Although the same side of the Moon always faces Earth, its illuminated portion appears to grow and shrink as the Moon moves around our planet. The eight phases are:.

Upcoming Moon — The moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (so, we don't see anything).

Waxing Crescent — A small sliver of light appears on the right side.

In a recent development, first Quarter — Half of the moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-moon.

Waxing Gibbous — More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon — The whole face of the moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous — The moon starts losing light on the right side.

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) — Another half-moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent — A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#3567. AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It

AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.
  • Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude.
  • Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.

Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude. While the conjecture, which describes how prime numbers are distributed, is widely assumed to be true, many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, and the problem has become something of a holy grail of number theory.

Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it. On Saturday, the nonprofit the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib stated on Saturday they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. The problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles, they confirmed. Now, “we look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the fresh ideas in this proof,” they wrote.

According to recent reports, lean proofs are written to be checked by machine, while mathematical papers are written to explain the results to the community so that they can be reviewed and advanced. But Alpöge hasn’t released the paper version, which clocks in at 250,000 pages and is, in his own estimation, a “travesty of slop.” (On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also said that the 250,000 pages was a “joke … I find substantial number [sic] extremely hilarious.”) That’s left mathematicians to their own devices as they try to decipher what fresh findings they can obtain and build from the result.

“Knowing there is a proof is one thing,” Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, tells WIRED, “but when we understand the proof, that would allow us to actually go beyond what has happened, to build fresh branches of mathematics perhaps or formulate the next conjecture to push the horizon further.”.

Recent findings suggest that saha reckons the community effort should be able to simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. But complicating this feat is the fact that the proof appears to draw on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. “I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human,” says Saha, “but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien, and that breaks our intuition about how very difficult mathematical results might come about.”.

Industry observers note that he was shocked to see even his own corner of number theory utilized by the proof, and has since been trying to understand how. Saha has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters like those presented at conferences and shorter documents. But there’s a limit to that approach.

“It may well be that no single person has the expertise to understand in detail every part of the proof,” he states.

More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to try to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform designed to facilitate the understanding of AI breakthroughs. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof, though platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. “I personally believe the picture we will get in the end, once the ideas of this proof have been properly understood, will be astoundingly beautiful," he tells WIRED.

Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof.

AI labs have previously been criticized for rushing to publish breakthrough mathematical results, claiming glory while leaving the academic community to digest the results—and clean up mistakes.

Recent findings suggest that “No human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document,” the Association for Human Mathematics, a group of more than 1,000 mathematicians founded in September, wrote in a statement on Friday of the 17-million-line opus. It complained that Alpöge’s announcement “builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way.”.

In a recent development, alpöge, who before joining Anthropic was a researcher at Harvard University, acknowledged on Friday what an “extraordinary” situation it was to present “the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighborhood around its mathematics,” and wrote that he would try his best to help digest the proof, including by writing it up properly. But having had to hold off from making the announcement ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, “I just could not live if I waited even longer,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, anthropic rival OpenAI in October proved a weaker version of the problem, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Alpöge had been scooped by OpenAI in September on another Millennium Prize Problem concerning the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe fluid motion. When the organization said it had solved part of the problem, Alpöge’s collaborator, Latest York University professor Tristan Buckmaster, claimed OpenAI had rushed ahead to beat the pair to it after becoming aware of his work. The pair also revealed on Friday that they had completed the remaining unsolved parts of the Navier-Stokes problem.

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Election Deniers Despair Because Even Donald Trump Isn’t Buying What They’re Selling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that with his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure.
  • But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.
  • In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He said he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.

But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.

In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.

Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.

Sources indicate that “We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” notes Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”.

These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.

“This is a carbon copy of 2020,” remarked Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.

The big difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.

Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.

On November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more key than the voter! President DJT.”.

Election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.

According to recent reports, “I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and noted the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”.

Ticktin also noted he would speak directly to Trump about the challenges and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”.

While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a fresh poll from UC San Diego.

Industry observers note that major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another plan: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.

It has been revealed that “Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne stated over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a upcoming election in 120 days.”.

But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype highlights off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the newly introduced HiLight LED in one.
  • I would much rather have the temperature sensor over the HiLight LED.
  • Images posted to Telegram (via NotebookCheck) show an apparent prototype of the Pixel 11 Pro XL.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype highlights off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the newly introduced HiLight LED in one.

I would much rather have the temperature sensor over the HiLight LED. I didn't use the temp sensor much but it was handy if whenever I was sick and wanted to check my temp without jamming an under tongue temp stick or wasting money on a temporal temp device -- because my phone already had one in it!

Images posted to Telegram (via NotebookCheck) show an apparent prototype of the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The device is seen with the markings that are common to other known Pixel prototypes, with the key difference compared to the final model being the fact that the camera bar has both a temperature sensor and HiLight.

We can tell this is HiLight due to the diffused rear LED, and we know this isn’t a Pixel 10 Pro XL because the camera bar has full-width glass instead of a metal portion.

Recent findings suggest that google pulled the plug on the temperature sensor in Pixel 11 Pro after the prior three generations offered the feature. While the sensor was never particularly beloved, Google did see backlash from the lack of functionality in HiLight at launch. Having both features may have resulted in a different sentiment around the updated hardware.

  • Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” claims the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”.

The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she says.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

The stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie says, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”.

Industry observers note that over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few issues that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

According to recent reports, “It's the latest generational beef,” says Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in Latest York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

Sources indicate that lundquist says the concern has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

As a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”.

Industry observers note that her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she states. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”.

Sources indicate that others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He indicates his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

“It can get heated,” states John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

Sources indicate that “Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” states Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those upcoming to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll said they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.).

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, says AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next massive step for every single person in the world.”.

In a recent development, debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke notes. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”.

“He wants what's best for me,” Luke states. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”.

According to recent reports, in the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”.

It has been revealed that when Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh indicates. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”.

It has been revealed that lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he indicates. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”.

In a recent development, his advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he indicates. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”.

Industry observers note that if you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he says. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”.

Sources indicate that intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he notes. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”.

  • Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app.
  • As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft revealed this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:.

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the new private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

Sources indicate that microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business customers. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

If you are trying to get your hands on a PlayStation 5 right now, the real win is not a discount — it is simply finding one in stock at standard retail price. Between a global RAM shortage driven by the AI boom, which pushed Sony to hike console prices twice in under a year, and the massive hype around GTA 6, standalone console markdowns are nowhere to be found.

In a recent development, today, the PS5 Slim Digital Edition starts at $599.99, and the flagship PS5 Pro retails for $899.99. Depending on the model, that means PlayStation 5 hardware actually costs $150 to $200 more today than it did when the console originally debuted in 2020.

For weeks, the hype around GTA 6 completely wiped out store shelves across the country — especially for the PS5 Pro. The good news is that major retailers like Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon are finally restocking standard PS5 models at regular list price.

We recommend paying full sticker price, because third-party marketplace listings are barely worth looking at anyway — the few that are up are mostly refurbished units marked up to nearly double the retail cost, so we left them off our list.

Even at full sticker price, picking up a PS5 or PS5 Pro makes a lot of sense if you are upgrading for GTA 6 or catching up on Sony's massive library of current-gen games.

Industry observers note that the standard PlayStation 5 Digital Edition gives you the core current-gen experience in a slim, compact design that fits easily into a media console. You get an 825GB ultra-high-speed SSD that cuts load screens to seconds, 4K TV output, up to 120 fps gameplay on supported titles, and Tempest 3D AudioTech. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Sources indicate that it also ships with Sony's DualSense wireless controller — featuring haptic feedback and adaptive triggers that add physical resistance when you pull a trigger or drive over rough terrain — and plays more than 8,500 backward-compatible PS4 games with smoother frame rates. Plus, if you ever decide you want to buy physical discs later, you can snap Sony's detachable disc drive right onto the side.

If you want the best possible visuals in Vice City, stepping up to the PlayStation 5 Pro unlocks PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) for sharper AI-upscaled clarity, upgraded GPU performance, and advanced ray tracing. While Rockstar confirmed GTA 6 targets 30 fps across all consoles at launch, the PS5 Pro is the only system that gets exclusive ray-traced shadows and cleaner image upscaling in the game.

Beyond GTA 6, dozens of major PS5 titles run at higher frame rates and sharper resolutions on the Pro, and its massive 2TB SSD easily swallows GTA 6's 212GB install size with plenty of storage left over for the rest of your library.

If you want to lock down a console while shelves still have stock, here is where the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro are currently available at standard retail price:.

Amazon — Along with the standalone PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB available at regular retail price, Amazon also has the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition (825GB) + DualSense Wireless Controller Bundle discounted by roughly $22 — the only actual bundle discount floating around major stores right now.

Best Buy — Both the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and the PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB are available to order online right now at list price.

Target — You can grab both the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and the PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB at standard retail price while current restocks last.

Walmart — The PlayStation 5 Digital Edition is back in stock directly from Walmart at regular retail price.

If you don't want to pay 2026's inflated brand-fresh sticker prices, look straight at PlayStation Direct's certified refurbished lineup. Sony sells official refurbished PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles for up to $100 less than brand-new units ($499.99 for the Digital Edition, $549.99 for the Disc Edition, and $849 for the PS5 Pro), backed by a full one-year manufacturer's warranty. It is the most reliable way to shave real money off the console without gambling on sketchy third-party resellers.

You might also spot occasional game bundles at significant-box stores, though availability is hit-or-miss. Even the overpriced bundles and double-the-price third-party listings floating around online are largely sold out, proving just how intense the demand still is.

After watching store shelves sit completely empty less than a week ago, seeing major retailers finally restock both the PS5 and PS5 Pro is a welcome surprise. If you are trying to jump into GTA 6 without paying double to a reseller, grab an official unit at retail price — or check PlayStation Direct's refurbished store — before this wave clears out too.
