📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise networks are under severe strain.
  • In a recent development, as AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows.
  • This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In partnership withTata Communications.

Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.

In a recent development, as AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study.

This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.

Key findings from the report include:.

According to recent reports, AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to customers. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.

According to recent reports, AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces latest approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.

According to recent reports, AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

It has been revealed that network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.

NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.

Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant fresh investment and complicate operations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is a massive pop culture event that is affecting a whole lot of people from a whole lot of different angles. Arguably, few are benefiting more from the game's launch last week than Carly Rae Jepsen.

It has been revealed that the Canadian pop star broke big worldwide with "Call Me Maybe" in 2012 and has followed up with an extremely respectable career that includes a devoted fanbase and eight studio albums, including the recently released Day & Night. However, one of her most beloved (and slightly less-well-known) songs is blowing up on streaming for the first time in a decade thanks to its inclusion in GTA 6, per Billboard Canada.

That would be "Run Away With Me," the opening track to Jepsen's highly acclaimed 2015 record Emotion. Aside from being featured on GTA 6's in-game radio station Flash FM, "Run Away With Me" also soundtracks an important early-game mission. According to Billboard and an X account called Carly Rae Jepsen Charts, the song was streamed more than 100,000 times on both Saturday and Sunday, its two biggest individual streaming days since the song was new.

In a recent development, to be clear, this is not necessarily a case of GTA breathing life into an obscure old song. "Run Away With Me" made a small splash on music charts in Canada and a handful of other territories back in 2015, and was a critical darling both at the time and now. But the GTA bump is clearly very real, nonetheless.

Warning: The following section contains spoilers for an early mission in GTA 6.

If you're curious as to the specific context in which "Run Away With Me" and its iconic distorted saxophone riff are used in GTA 6, allow me to explain. During the game's first story chapter, players will run into a mission called "Day Release" that involves protagonists Jason and Lucia going to a party on an expensive yacht. Lucia's parole ankle monitor is temporarily disabled for this mission, and the whole idea is that she and Jason get to have a fun day of rich people debauchery together for the first time since she got out of prison.

In a recent development, A few minutes into the mission, Jason and Lucia are invited to ride jet skis with the host of the yacht party, and this is where the "Run Away With Me" needle-drop happens. As the two lovers speed around the waters of a fictional Miami stand-in, Jepsen's catchy chorus reverberates throughout the action. The best part is that the mission keeps going and includes several little gameplay vignettes, most of which are scored by a longer remix of the song provided by Overmono and Pegassi.

What makes this great for those who enjoy both GTA and Carly Rae Jepsen is that the song isn't used just because it's good. It also perfectly evokes the excitement of the early stages of being in love and sonically fits the high-speed action during the mission.

Recent findings suggest that needless to say, it's been stuck in my head ever since I played the mission a few days ago. I hope it gets there for you, too. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one upcoming feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to.
  • The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
  • Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta declared a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one upcoming feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.

The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.

Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta declared a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.

WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.

But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.

According to recent reports, this problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to customers under 18.

Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into owners’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the tech giant introduced in 2025, are enabled.

Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.

Recent findings suggest that the new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him.
  • The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.
  • The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable tech giant as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug.

The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.

The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable tech giant as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.

It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. They argued the Nvidia founder was personally integral to the health of the US AI industry, and therefore the stock market and entire economy.

“Great men make great mistakes. But nobody has ever been like this, not Elon Musk, not anyone. All the success we’re enjoying, all the tech gains, that’s all down to one guy,” mentioned an ally of Huang.

But one of the most remarkable comebacks in corporate history, which called to mind Sam Altman’s brief ousting at OpenAI, still leaves the semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI boom in treacherous waters.

Nvidia and Huang face probes by the FBI and SEC, congressional investigations, and difficult questions over governance and Huang’s personal connections to a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in chip smuggling.

Even after gaining nearly $1 trillion in market value on the news of Huang’s return on Monday, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago.

Huang told employees on Monday he had “made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions, the people mentioned.

It has been revealed that trump personally spoke to the board in Huang’s defense, triggering an about-face days after it had categorically ruled out a return. The board noted it was confident Huang posed no national security risk after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” but that its internal investigation would continue.

The seeds of Huang’s comeback were sown within hours of his resignation on November 12, which came after reports of affairs with a firm executive and a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client called Megaspeed, now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

According to recent reports, allies in Silicon Valley rallied around him. A small group of Huang’s supporters, including Uber founder Travis Kalanick, venture capitalists Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner, and Marc Andreessen, as well as Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood, leapt to action, according to people familiar with the matter, making the case in public and in private for Huang’s reinstatement.

It has been revealed that andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. The other members of the group did not respond.

Within 24 hours of Huang’s resignation, Baker and Gerstner published an open letter to Nvidia’s board urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”.

Recent findings suggest that their effort had Huang’s backing, the FT reported last week. On Tuesday, Huang confirmed he was prepared to step back into the role.

While the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, publicly insisted Huang could not return, Kress spent last week looking to steady the ship with a strong quarterly earnings report and promises to expedite pay rises and equity grants as Nvidia shares plummeted. A organization “all-hands” meeting on Wednesday featured a show of unity from its top executive team, to the tune of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”.

Behind the scenes, Huang’s allies in his “kitchen cabinet” began lobbying the White House and other power brokers in Washington.

One arranged a phone call between Huang and Vance last week that lasted 45 minutes. During the conversation, Huang defended his positions on US semiconductor export controls and remote access to chips, and his dealings with Megaspeed.

Vance, a former venture capitalist who was mentored by Peter Thiel and has raised millions of dollars from Silicon Valley, was seemingly persuaded by the entreaties of Huang and his allies, who are probably a crucial source of funding if Vance decides to run for president.

“Everyone who was key in the tech world was beating his door down,” stated the person.

According to recent reports, “He wasn’t doing it to help raise dollars. That never even came up. But he clearly understands that half of US GDP depends on Nvidia right now… the Nasdaq is up 7 percent. If you think that’s happening without Jensen, you’re crazy,” they added.

​Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the company of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.

Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.

On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: “This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America.”.

Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so swiftly.

One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.

Sources indicate that “He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?” noted one.

Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 percent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.

“If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, ‘How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to fuck off next time,’” said one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.

It has been revealed that huang’s return does not signal an end to the company’s troubles. Trump on Monday noted the US attorney general’s office had “done a very thorough investigation” into Huang’s conduct and “exonerated” him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.

Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.

It has been revealed that no member of the cabinet apart from Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.

Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

One longtime associate of board chair Jones said the decision to reinstate Huang would do little to assuage public concern and market worries around AI.

Industry observers note that “The midterm elections showed that the wider public is deeply skeptical about all things AI,” the person said. “The Jensen affair masks a growing market consensus that the debt-leveraged speculative data center build-out is quite fragile.”.

It also does nothing to reduce scrutiny of Nvidia’s board, which is stacked with longtime Huang allies and lacks any major tech or national security figures.

“While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” Bernstein analysts wrote on Monday, adding that it “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other notable decisions.”.

In a recent development, others were more blunt. “Corporate governance has gone the way of the dodo,” said one large Nvidia investor.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two significant improvements that make it worth the upgrade.
  • In a recent development, precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item.
  • With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two significant improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

In a recent development, precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the latest speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era.
  • “Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s been a bumpy road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.

“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.

That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.

Sources indicate that “Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”.

Industry observers note that both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.

In a recent development, G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that manufacturer, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter stated.

The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.

“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter noted. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”.

In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a newly introduced generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.

Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.

“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so major that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he noted.

#3408. Tech Report: Why your smart TV keeps losing its Wi-Fi connection

Tech Report: Why your smart TV keeps losing its Wi-Fi connection

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smart TV can drop Wi-Fi for several reasons, and most of them have little to do with the TV.
  • In a recent development, it's not uncommon for smart TVs to struggle with a Wi-Fi connection, even if it's been relatively smooth sailing for a while.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's a little tougher for 5GHz Wi-Fi, however, which is faster than 2.4GHz but lacks range and struggles with passing through walls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smart TV can drop Wi-Fi for several reasons, and most of them have little to do with the TV.

In a recent development, it's not uncommon for smart TVs to struggle with a Wi-Fi connection, even if it's been relatively smooth sailing for a while. Things change, furniture gets moved around, routers are upgraded, fresh TVs are purchased and old TVs are moved to another room. Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 tri-band routers bring faster data rates to the table, but Wi-Fi 4 (2.4GHz and 5GHz dual-band support) is still the most prevalent Wi-Fi standard in the US. For the most part, 5GHz and 2.4GHz are enough for the average household, though it's ideal for most smart TVs to use 5GHz for 4K streaming.

Recent findings suggest that it's a little tougher for 5GHz Wi-Fi, however, which is faster than 2.4GHz but lacks range and struggles with passing through walls. Your router's features could be making things worse. Many routers use "band steering" when broadcasting Wi-Fi, a feature that combines bands under a single network name, switching your devices back and forth automatically. It sounds convenient. You want your device connected to the most stable band, but it can wreak havoc on your TV's Wi-Fi connection. Devices don't always get the right band, degrading your smart TV's connection stability and speed. For those with older smart TVs, the lack of compatibility could be hampering your connection as well. Older models may not support DFS channels and won't find networks using them.

Industry observers note that isolate the problem and figure out whether it's the TV or the network by connecting a phone or a laptop to the same Wi-Fi network. If it runs fine, the problem is probably with your smart TV. If not, check your router, gateway or your internet service first.

Sources indicate that next, check if there's a firmware or software waiting for installation in the TV's system settings. If there's an enhancement available but your internet connection isn't working, check the model name on the manufacturer's website to try and flash an update via USB stick instead.

Industry observers note that restarting could also be an easy fix. Unplug your TV for two minutes and the router for about a minute. Plug the router back in and let it reconnect before messing with the TV. If the problem persists, go into the TV's settings and clear out the saved connections. On your router settings, turn off band steering and give each available band its own name so you can choose which band the TV will use such as 36, 40, 44, or 48 instead of Auto. If the TV keeps dropping on 5GHz, set the band to a fixed channel outside the DFS range.

Industry observers note that most smart TV's default to a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi signal to avoid losing connection with your router. This band can interfere with special Bluetooth remote features like voice command, so try turning off the Bluetooth-reliant features on your remote. If Bluetooth is critical for accessibility reasons, switch the TV to 5GHz, bring the router closer, or go the direct route with an Ethernet cable.

Several factors go into this, including signal strength, network congestion, router placement and the TV's capabilities. If the signal is strong, the obvious choice is 5GHz. Switch to 2.4GHz only if the TV is too far from the router to hold a steady connection with 5GHz.

Recent findings suggest that speed and crowding are typical issues in most homes because everybody has a device or ten that connects to the internet. A 4K stream needs a steady 20 Mbps (Netflix suggests 15 Mbps, but 20+ is preferable). 2.4GHz has a longer range and handles walls better, but it's slower and usually more congested because neighboring routers, microwaves and Bluetooth devices can all interfere with it. Once you've eliminated band steering and renamed your bands, try each one out. Use your TV's network status screen to make a signal strength comparison.

Consider a wired connection. A close router makes this option more feasible, so you don't have to run an Ethernet cable across ceilings and under baseboards. If there's just too much space and you can't shrink the gap between the router and TV, a mesh network is another viable alternative. Most mesh nodes have Ethernet ports, so you can place one near your TV and run an Ethernet cable from the mesh to the TV. Just make sure your mesh network has a strong connection.

#3407. Industry News: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2116 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought.
  • Sources indicate that the chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in.
  • Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China’s Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that’s vital to the story of how our genus, Homo, took over the world.

Sources indicate that the chemical makeup of the teeth’s enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we’d previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans.

Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth.

In a recent development, proteins in teeth are sturdier than DNA, so they’re more likely to survive a few hundred thousand years. But like DNA, proteins contain variations that can help identify the species they came from. Four of the five teeth in the study had distinctly Homo erectus proteins in their enamel; the fifth seems to be some other hominin species, most likely a Denisovan (more on that below).

Sources indicate that the hominin teeth and the thousands of animal bone fragments had accumulated in a cement-like rock called breccia. Based on luminescence dating (a method that measures how long it’s been since mineral grains were last exposed to sunlight) of the cave sediments, along with the ratios of uranium isotopes in the bones themselves, it looks like that breccia formed sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. That’s a wide range, but it’s enough to show that Homo erectus lived in what’s now southern China at least 60,000 years longer than we’ve previously realized.

Homo erectus emerged in Africa sometime before 2 million years ago, and they had reached East and Southeast Asia—including the islands of Indonesia—by around 1.7 million years ago. The most recent Homo erectus fossils anywhere else in mainland Asia date to somewhere between 420,000 and 400,000 years ago. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java, however, reveal that Homo erectus held on in the islands up until at least 177,000 to 108,000 years ago. That makes it a little surprising that nobody had found traces of Homo erectus on the mainland during that 200,000- to 300,000-year gap.

These nine teeth help fill in some of that gap, showing that Homo erectus was still around on the mainland all that time after all. On its own, that would be nontrivial, but the teeth also shed light on how these long-dead hominins lived, what the world around them looked like, and how this handful of hominins was related to the rest of their species. And it turns out we’ve been drastically underestimating Homo erectus.

Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University Credit: Kira Westaway, Macquarie University.

Four of the five teeth that Welker and his colleagues sequenced proteins from clearly belonged to Homo erectus. Careful measurements of the other four—things like the shape and dimensions of the crown, the roots, and the place where the outer layer of enamel meets the inner layer of dentine—suggest these also belonged to Homo erectus.

But the ninth tooth, from Baxian, has proteins that don’t match any known Homo erectus variants, and the shape also looks decidedly un-Homo–erectus-like, “strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than Homo erectus in Baxian Cave,” wrote Welker and his colleagues in their recent paper in the journal Nature.

In a recent development, but who were those other hominins? The enigmatic ninth tooth looks like it belonged to a Denisovan (or Homo longi, if you prefer). But Welker and his colleagues can’t be absolutely sure, because its proteins don’t exactly match any known Denisovan sequence, either (and there’s no clearly identified Denisovan lower second molar enamel-dentine junction to compare it to). But we do know that Denisovans lived in the wider region of mainland Asia at the time, based on fossils from other sites, and there’s no evidence of any other species running around at the same time.

“It therefore seems plausible that the Homo erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian Cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins,” wrote Welker and his colleagues.

Recent findings suggest that now, to clarify, Naxian and Baxian Caves weren’t (as far as anyone knows) places where hominins actually lived. The bones and teeth there seem to have been carried in by porcupines, with the result that “why do porcupines collect bones?” is now part of your faithful correspondent’s search history [EDITOR’S NOTE: my search history now includes “there are porcupines in China?”]. So the presence of this tooth doesn’t mean that Homo erectus and Denisovans were roommates. But it does mean they were living in the same general area at around the same time; based on the territorial habits of modern porcupines, the teeth probably came from within an area of less than 100 square kilometers. So there’s a nonzero chance that Homo erectus and Denisovans might have interacted in some way, although we have no way to know what that interaction might have looked like.

Not long after this, our species demonstrated up in the area, and we know for a fact that our species interacted, ahem, very closely with Denisovans in this part of the world. Exactly when Homo sapiens arrived is still a matter of some debate, but some fossils from southern China that may be Homo sapiens date as far back as 100,000 or 120,000 years ago, before the major out-of-Africa migration. So for a brief period of time, there may have been at least two and maybe three species of hominins living in the rainforests of what’s now southern China.

Sources indicate that while the enamel proteins from four of the Baxian and Naxian teeth are clearly Homo erectus, they have a slightly different version of one particular protein—one amino acid swapped for another in the sequence that makes up the protein ameloblastin. This variant is clearly different from every other Asian Homo erectus fossil with proteins that researchers have sequenced. That means they’re probably part of a different genetic population (a group of hominins that live in the same area and mostly interbred among themselves).

Sources indicate that there are a handful of other Homo erectus fossils from elsewhere in Asia that share one amino acid substitution with these four, but the Baxian and Naxian ones have another substitution that the other four don’t have, which means that at some point, their population branched off from the others. By plotting that kind of information on what’s called a phylogenetic tree, anthropologists can begin to map out how different groups of Homo erectus are related and how they may have moved around in time and space. And what we’re learning is pretty cool.

“The phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population [at Baxian and Naxian Caves] might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans,” wrote Welker and his colleagues. That divergence happened more than 600,000 years ago. And half a millennium after that, it seems, one group of Homo erectus still living in southern Asia may have met some long-lost cousins.

Isotopes of the chemical elements carbon and oxygen in the enamel of not just the Homo erectus teeth, but teeth from several animal species like elephants (both the pygmy Stegodon and the full-size version), rhinos, apes, and relatives of modern cattle, strongly point to the area around Baxian and Naxian Caves having been a densely canopied tropical rainforest during the Middle Pleistocene.

Recent findings suggest that different types of plants use slightly different chemical processes to do photosynthesis, so they end up with different amounts of the isotopes carbon-12 and carbon-13; the ratios of those isotopes in the teeth of whatever ate the plants (in this case, pygmy elephants and Homo erectus, among others) can reveal the makeup of the local environment. At Baxian and Naxian Caves, those ratios point to a forest where the trees’ upper branches form a thick, closed canopy above the forest floor. Westaway and her colleagues say the signals look very similar to rainforests in the Amazon Basin today.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the ratio of two oxygen isotopes, oxygen-18 and oxygen-16, can shed light on ancient climate conditions; higher amounts of oxygen-18, like the ones in all five teeth from Baxian and Naxian Caves, tend to signal warmer, wetter climates. All of those clues together point to tropical rainforest, a challenging environment that most anthropologists had previously assumed that only Homo sapiens were clever and adaptable enough to make a living in.

That idea, that we were the only hominins capable of making a go of it in tropical rainforests, was so entrenched that it has been considered a possible explanation for the lack of Homo erectus fossils in southern Asia after about 400,000 years ago. Around this time, the climate became warmer and wetter, allowing dense, closed-canopy tropical rainforests to spread.

“In southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of […] expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-Homo sapiens hominin taxa, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savanna-woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues.

Even on Java, where Homo erectus lasted until almost 100,000 years ago, those last groups seem to have lived in small patches of more open woodlands, while rainforests spread across the rest of the islands—another correlation that gives anthropologists reason to think the spread of rainforests may have had a hand in the extinction of Homo erectus.

In a recent development, however, the evidence from Baxian and Naxian Caves suggests Homo erectus could survive in the rainforest, “even if such habitats did not represent its primary ecological niche,” as Westaway and her colleagues put it. That doesn’t mean that every group of Homo erectus was as successful at adapting to spreading rainforests—it’s safe to assume there were cultural and social differences among the groups that might have made some more adaptable than others. But it does mean that we’ve been drastically underestimating our late cousins, and we may need to rethink what we’ve assumed were the limits of their world.

Other evidence in the enamel of the Baxian and Naxian Caves teeth underscores that point, revealing that a few of these Homo erectus individuals spent their childhoods as much as 250 kilometers away from the cave where their teeth ended up. Bedrock in different places has different ratios of the isotopes strontium-87 and strontium-86; plants take up dissolved strontium through their roots, and eventually it replaces some of the calcium in the bones (or tooth enamel) of the animals that eat the plants. So the ratio of strontium isotopes in your bones can be traced to the area of bedrock where your food was grown during the final years of your life, while the ratio in your tooth enamel is a souvenir of the bedrock where your food was grown when you were around 2 to 6 years old and forming your adult teeth. (Modern food systems are going to be a massive headache for future archaeologists.).

Recent findings suggest that all four Homo erectus teeth that Westaway and her colleagues studied suggested that their erstwhile owners had either moved around between different areas or ate food gathered from different areas when they were very young. Some of those strontium ratios match bedrock as far away as northern Vietnam, about 250 kilometers away from Baxian and Naxian Caves, mostly through closed-canopy rainforest.

In other words, a handful of teeth offer enough fragments of a story to show us “that Homo erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments and that long-distance mobility into those environments may have been a common behavioral pattern rather than exceptional behavior by isolated individuals,” wrote Westaway and her colleagues. “Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question.”.

Tech Report: David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.
  • Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.
  • In a recent development, though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.

Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.

In a recent development, though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.

It has been revealed that following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who noted on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”.

Recent findings suggest that others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the organization’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.

It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.

Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.

Recent findings suggest that at least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.

Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the tech giant was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.

Sources indicate that netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the firm’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

Why the FAA doesn't want you to put AirPods in your luggage

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Air travel rules treat one part of your AirPods differently, and knowing where to pack them can save you some trouble on your next trip.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Anyone who's flown in the US is well aware of how fickle passenger rules can be. It's only in 2025 that passengers got to stop taking off their shoes during security screenings, and other rules seem to be applied inconsistently. Though some electronics are definite red flags for the TSA, it's possible that screeners at one airport could insist you take a gadget out of your bag, while the crew at another fumes at you for holding up the line. Or vice versa.

Believe it or not, AirPods are another potential point of controversy, despite them being virtually omnipresent because of the iPhone and their noise-canceling capabilities. You should actually be fine bringing them with you to watch movies or listen to podcasts. Instead, the issue is whether or not you can stash them in checked luggage.

You might think that would be an innocuous move, but the reality is the opposite, at least if you read the letter of the law. There is some justification, too: the lithium-ion battery in your AirPods' charging case could, in a worst-case scenario, catch fire in the cargo hold, where crews can't easily reach it.

Sources indicate that according to the Transportation Security Administration, which in turn cites Federal Aviation Administration rules, the main issue is your AirPods' charging case. TSA rules bar you from checking lithium-ion batteries for a variety of electronics, including "portable rechargers and power banks," no matter if they're rated at 100Wh or less of capacity. You may also be barred from checking some other devices with built-in batteries, such as cordless curling irons and e-cigarettes. Don't expect to check your AirPods Max 2 just because it doesn't need a case.

The threat, according to the FAA, is the prospect of thermal runaway. If a lithium-ion battery overheats, takes damage or is simply exposed to water, there's a risk that it'll catch fire mid-flight, and it would be hard to tackle if it's deep within a cargo hold. Worse, lithium fires are notoriously resistant to conventional firefighting methods. Crews may need to douse the battery with water, since a conventional halon extinguisher can put out the flames but can't cool the cells enough to stop the fire from reigniting.

Sources indicate that is there a high chance of thermal runaway with your AirPods case? Probably not. Apple tends to maintain high manufacturing standards, and AirPods cases are durable, able to survive plenty of jolts and drops. But all it would take is one fluke to result in tragedy, which is presumably why the TSA and FAA have a strict policy regardless of brand. There's at least some chance of smothering or isolating a fire if you've got AirPods in your carry-on.

Recent findings suggest that while there are too many international regulations to touch on, as far as the US goes, you should plan on bringing all of your battery devices in carry-on baggage if they're not being worn, from AirPods and power banks to your laptop. That includes anything you're taking as a gift. For personal grooming, you can save yourself a lot of trouble by putting together a completely non-electric travel kit. Hotel rooms do often include their own hair dryers, you know.

When you reach security screening, don't split hairs if you want to save time. If it's electronic, take it off your wrist, off your head or out of your pocket, and leave it loose in the provided bin(s). You should always remove laptops, tablets and e-readers from their bags and sleeves, no matter if a previous airport let you get away with keeping them in. The worst that can happen is that you'll need more bins, and that you'll take a few moments longer putting things back when screening is done.

According to recent reports, if there's any doubt about whether a device or accessory is flight-legal, it's best to either check the TSA's website or leave it at home. In fact, you can save yourself even more trouble by reducing the number of gadgets with you to the bare minimum. You'll probably want your AirPods, but if you're already taking your phone and laptop with you, you can leave your iPad and Steam Deck behind, which will speed up screening and make packing and charging less complicated.
